Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly gaining importance in the defence industry, with countries such as China and the United States (U.S.) actively investing in military applications. This has raised urgent ethical questions about the (mis)use of military AI, a topic rendered both more difficult and more important in the context of great power rivalry.1 In a context where Beijing is increasingly seeking to shape global AI governance, it is urgent to understand the perspectives of Chinese officials, scholars, and military strategists on the norms of applying AI in warfare.2 The Chinese debate on the ethics of military AI carries weight beyond China’s borders, as military powers across the world seek to adapt extant ethical frameworks to a new technological reality.3 Whilst these issues are widely discussed in international fora, such as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW),4 global  society is struggling to address the thorny ethical issues arising as machines start supplementing human cognition on the battlefield. If left unchecked, the uncertainties and vulnerabilities brought about by AI technologies could become a source of global instability.5 This is perceived even more acutely as AI starts offering the promise of battlefield advantage over adversaries. At this juncture, an assessment of the Chinese position on the future of warfare is long overdue. The Chinese government has been eager to embrace AI, and considers this essential to the global economic and military power competition.6 AI technologies in China already have a wide range of applications in the civilian realm, including for instance, its extensive civilian surveillance apparatus.7 Accompanying the enthusiasm in applying AI to the domestic sphere, is a parallel effort at shaping the concurrent international normative frameworks. Efforts at ensuring a global regulatory regime more in line with China’s political principles are also grounded in an increasingly active Chinese debate over the ethical frameworks of AI, with government agencies, think tanks and private entities weighing in.8 Since 2017, Beijing has published numerous documents that provide a window into the political drivers underpinning Chinese debates on AI.9 Domestically, emerging technologies and technological innovation are viewed as central to advancing national security and promoting the country’s modernization. Internationally, China aims to achieve primacy in AI innovation over the next decade. While the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) growing role as an international normshaper in a variety of fields has already seen a considerable amount of scholarship,10 Chinese views on military AI are still under-researched. Because of China’s role as an emerging AI powerhouse, the Chinese position on the normative boundaries of the future battlefield is thus a question of urgent interest. Not only does the topic go to the heart of Chinese efforts at agenda-setting for emerging technologies globally, but the potentially wide-ranging military capabilities powered by AI make the topic particularly consequential. The article will address this issue through analysing the Chinese debates on the ethics of military AI, addressing the research question: ‘How do the Chinese elites frame the ethics of military AI in public sources?’. The investigation describes how Chinese actors narrate and prioritize ethical concerns, identifying recurring patterns and themes across sources. ‘Ethics’ is in this context defined as referring to debates on the proper constraints, responsibilities, and normative principles guiding AI in warfare. In the Chinese debate, ethical considerations are often articulated in strategic or governance-oriented language, reflecting a close intertwining of normative reasoning and policy  priorities. Chinese sources often highlight differences in state—citizen relations compared to liberal democratic contexts, framing these divergences as part of a broader ‘value competition’ over AI under the influence of geopolitics. It is important to note, however, that both Western and Chinese debates encompass internal diversity; this analysis focuses on dominant patterns rather than treating either side as monolithic. In doing so, the article provides the first systematic mapping of how ethical reasoning around AI in warfare is framed domestically in China, thereby extending and differentiating from studies of China’s broader AI ethics discourse. China’s position on general ethical AI and AI safety is covered by existing literature.11 Furthermore, existing scholarship has extensively examined the ethical challenges of AI and autonomous weapons,12 focusing primarily on Western debates or technical-operational issues. This article’s contribution builds on this body of work, but shifts the focus to Chinese domestic debates, which remain underexplored in the literature. The article will first provide a broad overview of Beijing’s position on AI, and how it ties into the role of this technology in military planning. The main section of the article then engages in-depth with the Chinese domestic debate on the ethics of military AI. Here, three key principles of China’s views on the ethics of military AI are identified, namely: the de-universalization of AI ethics, pointing towards the potential of differing ethical spheres in emerging technologies; the importance of ensuring the primacy of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) control—and hence human control— over military decision-making; and the use of ambiguity in international cooperation to uphold the primacy of national security. In conclusion the article argues that these dominant principles of the debate are likely to shape the possibilities of a more aligned international normative framework on military AI in a manner that could show a way towards limited forms of AI arms control, but that China’s posture relative to Western positions in the ongoing efforts to shape the future of AI-assisted warfare leaves substantial hurdles to be overcome. In providing the first scholarly mapping and analysis of the domestic Chinese debate on military AI, sources were selected if they met at least one of three criteria: (1) formal authority (e.g. government or PLA institutions), (2) explicit articulation of policies or ethical frameworks, or (3) broad circulation and citation in Chinese scholarly and policy debates. This article’s dataset therefore includes publicly available Chinese-language sources directly addressing military AI ethics, supplemented by widely referenced general AI ethics texts where they explicitly touch on military applications.13 In total, the dataset consists of 50 textual primary sources, comprising official policy documents, PLA-affiliated commentaries, and academic writings (see the Appendix for a full list). The ‘elites’ of this public discourse are defined as political leaders, military-affiliated scholars and strategists, and academic/technical experts with recognized influence on policy debates. Amongst the latter category, figures such as Zeng Yi, widely cited below, is representative of this group of academic actors whose writings shape domestic discussions and international AI ethics forums, though they are not political or military decision-makers. The key overarching themes—de-universalization of AI ethics, Primacy of the Party Man, and balancing national security with international cooperation—were identified through inductive source-analysis.14 Rather than relying solely on frequency, the analysis thus considers patterns of emphasis, conceptual significance, and their recurrence across sources, through an iterative and exploratory process were the analytical categories were reiterated and adjusted until identifying those with the widest degree of saturation, namely those reflecting the underpinning themes of the  widest array of the source material.15 Political and military discourses are, for example, not identical. Political elites tend to frame AI ethics in terms of governance and legitimacy, while military-affiliated scholars emphasize operational control and battlefield risks. The three key themes identified thus represent thematic overlaps across elite discourses rather than wholly coherent or unified positions. While much scholarship has examined China’s general approach to AI ethics,16 this article isolates the military dimension and synthesizes debates across political, military, and academic actors. Achieving an exhaustive mapping of the domestic Chinese debate on military AI ethics, entailed a rigorous, multi-stage process of source identification. First, official policy documents were collected from the most relevant Chinese government actors, including the State Council, the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Science and Technology, the Central Military Committee (CMC), and the Cyber Administration of China (CAC), by searching their websites.17 The keywords used in all searches are ‘rengong zhineng’ (artificial intelligence) combined with ‘junshi’ (military) and ‘lunli’ (ethics).18 This search was also extended to other relevant Ministries, such as the Ministry of Education, and provincial governments of key military-industrial bases, such as Shaanxi, Hubei, and Guizhou. However, across all the websites of relevant actors, the full text search for the keyword yielded a total of less than 10 hits. This article’s analysis is therefore based on all documents that deal directly with issues around the ethics of AI in the context of the battlefield, as well as drawing on documents that have a more general orientation (i.e. China’s national plan for AI development, or China’s position on the ethics of AI in the civilian domain), extrapolating the sections that refer to the military domain more specifically. Even where sources such as the Beijing AI Principles are not explicitly military, they are analysed insofar as they contain direct references to military applications or have been mobilized by Chinese actors to inform military AI ethics debates. Second, in order to capture a more complete scope of the evolving debate on military AI, especially in the absence of a public People’s Liberation Army (PLA) policy on intelligentied warfare, this article also draws upon the analysis of the most cited academic journals on the topic, drawn from the Chinese journal database CNKI.19 The search for ‘rengong zhineng + junshi + lunli’ yielded a total of 199 hits, of which 45 in the disciplines of military affairs, China politics and international politics, and ethics.20 As other China scholars have previously argued, this analysis also maintains that while not all sources possess the same level of authority, and are not exhaustive of the whole range of existing perspectives of the Chinese leadership on the matter, they collectively enable an exploration of the ongoing debates among Chinese elites.21 As with any database-driven sampling, the authors recognize the risk of coding errors and selection biases. To minimize these risks, the analysis process included iteratively cross-checking retrieved materials and focusing on patterns that recur across multiple sources. Whilst recognizing patterns of diversity of perspectives among the relevant Chinese actors, the corpus of sources is currently too narrow to allow for a sustained analysis of variations within the sub-groups of the elite discussion on military AI ethics—along the lines of the excellent research undertaken on the far broader corpus of texts on general AI ethics. Thus the most methodologically valid research design has been to identify the perspectives that are in common across the entire body of sources. The resulting dataset should therefore be read as capturing dominant and widely circulated positions rather than as an exhaustive account. Given that  discussions about AI and its ethical implications are relatively recent, authoritative sources can be found only from 2017, the materials used in the analysis below are dated 2017- October 2025. Finally, while there is no shortage of official documents and scholarly works in China that discuss general AI ethics or explore the technical applications of AI to military and security domains, there is a striking paucity of public sources explicitly addressing the ethics of military AI. This imbalance likely reflects structural features of China’s political system: ethical discussions in sensitive areas such as warfare are tightly managed, with the Party-state prioritizing strategic messaging and national security considerations over open-ended normative debate. As a result, ethical issues are often embedded indirectly within governance, control, or technical discourses rather than articulated in a stand-alone manner. Recognizing this asymmetry is crucial for understanding both the opportunities and the limits of China’s engagement with international debates on the ethics of AI in warfare. The Role of AI in the PLA and China’s Military-Civil Fusion Beijing relies heavily on AI to boost the modernization of its defence sector. In 2017, President Xi urged the military to ‘accelerate the development of military intelligentization, improve joint operations capabilities and combat capabilities based on network information systems’, viewing AI as critical to ensure future victory on the battlefield.22 In this context, intelligentized warfare can be defined as the operationalization of AI and AI-enabling technologies for military applications, including cloud computing, big data analytics, quantum computing, and autonomous systems.23 Current developments in the field of AI and its military applications within China focus on robotic and unmanned systems developed by the land, sea and air branches of the PLA; advanced missiles with precision guidance and limited autonomy; and several other domains including AI wargaming and decision-support functions; space, cyber, electronic, and psychological warfare; command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence (C4i) applications; situation awareness; and target recognition.24 Generally, while China so far has not built robotic weapons systems that can identify and engage targets without human intervention, several of its existing systems may be enabled to do so with software modifications.25 Thus, efforts seem to be directed mostly at improving the effectiveness of existing systems by equipping them with further autonomy, although the country is also looking into developing new and more innovative systems.26 The trajectory in both the development and employment of AI-enabled and autonomous weapons systems is uncertain, at least based on publicly available sources.27 However, there is a concern that the desire for battlefield advantage could push China to develop weapons systems with high degrees of autonomy, especially if the PLA views such weapons as necessary tools to compete with, or confront, other militaries.28 Furthermore, the Chinese military lacks contemporary operational experience, which may lead to mistakes or  unrealistic expectations about the use of technology in war. Chinese military scientists and researchers are debating such issues, and conversations around safety and technical concerns are also imbued with reflections on legal and ethical implications.

Delegating lethal decisions, fully or in part, to machines necessarily carries some fundamental risks for human rights or societal safety.29 A rich debate has ensued in Western academia, policymaking, and industry that attempts to tackle such challenges.30 Countries around the world have started to put forward their recommendations for the ethical use of military AI. The U.S. and the EU were taking the lead in this effort, and converging toward a shared framework for an ethical use of AI in the military—or at least this is the goal of current efforts.31 Both seem to emphasize the need to achieve a global consensus on shared norms and values, something that China, as demonstrated in this article, has reservations towards. Through frameworks including the Global AI Governance Initiative and the Global Data Security Initiative, China promotes ‘cyber sovereignty’ and highlights the benefits of AI for preserving social stability.32 In particular, the Global AI Governance Initiative, aimed at tracing the contours of global AI governance from Beijing’s perspective, was greeted in China as offering ‘an open, inclusive and fair approach for the development, security and governance of emerging artificial intelligence technologies and services, in stark contrast to the US’ restrictions and blockade aimed at preserving its hegemony’.33
The CMC has so far not released any policy clarifying priorities in the field of AI, and the PLA has similarly not established clear policies on issues of autonomy and AI yet

.34 Nonetheless, Chinese scholars envision AI and intelligent weapons as playing an important if not decisive role in future warfare.35 Despite concerns over an AI arms race expressed in public documents, most of China’s military leadership views the use of AI for military purposes as inevitable.36 However,

.37 This sentiment is reflected in the official position papers of the  Department of Arms Control of the Chinese MFA.38 Most recently, the MFA issued a new official statement in July 2025, further elaborating China’s position on the ethical governance of military AI. This document reiterates Beijing’s emphasis on human control, sovereignty, and the need for international cooperation under UN-centred frameworks, while continuing to resist universalist ethical standards.39 Not unlike their Western counterparts, Chinese scholars have argued that the increased use of unmanned combat in the future might challenge international humanitarian law; lower the threshold for initiating conflict; and weaken moral constraints on the battlefield.40

In line with increased Chinese clout and willingness to pro-actively shape global norms and institutions, there is a growing need to expand the framework for assessing China’s level of support for these norms, in ways that account for China’s move from a de facto norms taker, or breaker, to that of a norm shaper.41 Upon analysing commentaries and academic articles by military strategists and experts, three areas were identified that appear crucial to Chinese normative deliberations concerning the use of AI in war. These are, namely: wariness of universal ethical standards; maintaining Party and human control; and the strategic use of normative ambiguity to balance international cooperation with national security imperatives.42 In the following sub-sections, these three themes are analysed, explicating why they are key to understanding China’s position on the ethics of AI in the future battlefield.

Among the Beijing AI Principles, the section on ‘harmony and cooperation’ prescribes that ‘we should actively cooperate to establish an interdisciplinary, cross-disciplinary, cross-sectoral, crossagency, cross-regional, global and integrated AI governance ecosystem, avoid malicious competition, share governance experiences, and jointly respond to the impact of artificial intelligence with the philosophy of optimizing symbiosis’.43 Harmony and symbiosis are key terms defining the Chinese approach to AI ethics. Given the nebulous nature of the terms, a broader view of the source material is necessary in order to unpack the terms and their significance for Chinese views on military AI. The leading author of the Beijing AI Principles, Zeng Yi, is a key figure in the Chinese debate, not only through his domestic position, as he is one of the most central contributors to debates on topics of AI ethics,44 but also as a member of the UNESCO Ad Hoc Expert Group on Recommendation on the  Ethics of Artificial Intelligence where he has been actively promoting Chinese concepts in international AI ethics frameworks.45 In Zeng’s academic writings on AI standards, these concepts are linked to his view that in order to build a global AI governance regime, one should ‘recognize the significance of each country and institution’s proposal’, with a focus not on obtaining ‘unified AI guidelines’ but rather ‘on a more harmonious and complementary way to link different AI standards proposals, to make them orderly and consistent locally, while different standards proposals can still interact and be negotiated globally, with the goal to ultimately achieve harmonious complementarity and optimizing symbiosis’.46 This approach to localized AI norms also informs the ‘Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles’ initiative, which aims at ‘integrating, synthesizing, analyzing, and promoting global Artificial Intelligence Principles and their social and technical practices worldwide . . . [as well as] at understanding in which degree do these different AI Principles proposals share common values, differ and complete each other’.47 In an interview with National Science Review, Zeng points out how the cultural aspect plays a central role in China’s approach to AI: ‘In traditional Chinese philosophy, we have “be in Harmony, yet be different”. We adopt this principle to coordinate AI governance among different cultures’.48 When applied to the field of technology, Chinese traditional ethics points to ‘negotiation and adjustment of relationships between human beings, society and technology’.49 Similarly, other scholars have argued that the country should ‘accelerate the development of military-civil integrated artificial intelligence with Chinese characteristics’.50 Correspondingly, China’s 2021 position paper on ‘Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI)’ emphasizes the need to ‘observe national or regional ethical norms in the development, deployment and use of relevant weapon systems’.51 One article explicitly criticizes Western philosophical models as ‘highly abstract’ and disconnected from battlefield realities, and thus insufficient for guiding the dynamic ethics of military AI. Instead, drawing on Marxist dialectics, it is argued that military AI needs to be framed as part of a historical-materialist evolution of labor, tools, and systems.52

In turn, when translated into policy, references to harmony and relationality in the context of AI thus appear to be yet another iteration of China’s Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, whereby peaceful coexistence is premised upon respect of the sovereignty of the state. This

The idea of ‘optimizing symbiosis’ might therefore suggest that China will want to play an active role in establishing principles and standards for the development and regulation of AI technology, whilst insisting on its prerogative to enact norms with Chinese characteristics. This principle thus stands in tension to the universality principle embodied in international norms, such as the UNESCO’s Recommendations on the Ethics of AI, which aim ‘to provide a universal framework of values, principles and actions to guide States’.54 The de-universalized ethical approach to setting normative frameworks for AI carries obvious echoes of the ‘splinternet’ arising from China’s enormous efforts to keep the Chinese internet sphere under the government’s control—and the concurrent efforts at promoting ‘internet sovereignty’.55 Military matters are already hallmarked by being the field in which states are the most intransigent on allowing international oversight. Thus, given that the Chinese ethical approach to civilian AI is framed in anti-universalist terms, one should expect it to be all the more challenging for China to agree to binding universal norms for military AI.

These considerations seem to indicate that achieving military superiority should not come at the expense of societal safety.

Liang Jie from the National Defence University adds that it is necessary to follow the laws of war to ensure that intelligentized operations do not ‘turn against humanity’. He also raises the issue of legal responsibility and accountability as one that deserves special attention.60 Zeng Yi suggests that it is becoming increasingly difficult to ensure that AI systems achieve the original aims they were programmed for by humans; in particular, he points to risks that some military applications of AI may become a threat to society, and thus calls for a total ban on lethal autonomous weapons.61  Furthermore, in an interview with China Science Report, Zhou Zhihua from Nanjing University argues that ‘autonomous weapons are not ethical and not in the interest of mankind’.62

Advances in weapons systems are described as ‘autonomous’ (zizhu) or ‘intelligentized’ (zhinenghua). At a technical level, ‘autonomy’ can be enabled by different techniques and is not necessarily synonymous with the use of AI.65 Furthermore, discussions among military strategists and scientists seem to privilege the use of the terms ‘AI weapons’ and ‘intelligentized weapons’ (zhinenghua wuqi) over the term ‘autonomous weapons’ (zizhu wuqi), which is more prevalent in academic and technical texts. This difference is significant in that it suggests an emphasis on the ‘intelligence’ of weapons systems.66 Chinese academics debate whether LAWS will lead to ‘machine proxy wars’ and discuss some of the challenges to the laws of armed conflict, mostly related to responsibility and liability; the ability to distinguish between civilians and combatants; and the problems with ‘transferring’ decision-making from humans to machines.67 Others also point to the risks that autonomous weapons pose to civilians in ‘algorithmic warfare’ (suanfa zhanzheng).68

An efficient use of AI to speed up battlefield decision making, stands in tension to the particularly hierarchical nature and the strong political guidance inherent to the Chinese chain of command.69 This reluctance to relinquish control over information flows as well as decision making, even in the civilian sector, is most recently exemplified by the efforts at ensuring that the latest generation of AIdriven chatbots embody ‘the core socialist values’.70 President Xi clearly stated that the Party’s ‘absolute leadership’ over the army should be upheld as China embraces a ‘new military revolution’ brought about by science and technology.71 In this context, the military should continue to be subject to the will of the Party. President Xi argued that the Party’s ‘absolute leadership’ over the  army should be upheld as China embraces what he calls a ‘new military revolution’ brought about by science and technology.72 Such a relationship between the Party and the military is mirrored in debates on AI-enabled autonomous weapons, which, albeit to different degrees and sometimes indirectly, include ethical reflections on maintaining human control over machines. This may have been a contributing factor to the increased Chinese interest in seeking dialogue with the U.S. about the risks of autonomous weapons systems.73 Following Mao’s adage that political power grows from the barrel of a gun, the CCP seems skeptical of anything that may weaken the Party’s grip of the gun—be it man or machine.74 Nonetheless, in the military context, this has so far not stopped conversations over the presence of humans in, on, or out of the loop, and the army generally seems to have fewer negative reactions to humans on (rather than in) the loop than their civilian leaders.75 Overall, though, when the trends of the ‘mechanization of humans’ and the ‘humanization of machines’ are discussed, the human is always considered the ‘leader’ in the man-machine relationship.76 The papers reviewed here thus indicate a broad-based unease about high degrees of autonomy in military applications of AI, reflecting ethical concerns of human control over lethal battlefield platforms, as well as a general concern over the potential for increased autonomy to weaken the political leadership over military actions. Ambiguously Balancing International Cooperation and National Security The third factor emerging from discussions over the ethics of military AI in China is the use of ambiguity to balance between the benefits of engaging in international cooperation and the primal importance of the current push to modernize the military. As an example of such tension, the most debated issue in existing publications in China is LAWS, especially those operating with the support of AI technologies. Several academic papers provide an overview of the current state of global governance of AI military applications, particularly in the context of the CCW. These typically also include recommendations for how China should position itself in the debate, and many scholars agree that China should continue to ‘uphold multilateralism’,77 and ‘actively participate in the global discussion around LAWS arms control under the CCW framework and manage and control the strategic risks and the related ethical and legal challenges’.78 Participating in these conversations is said to be ‘in line with China’s national interests and conducive to grasping the initiative in rule-making’, based on the need to ‘balance humanitarian concerns and legitimate military and security needs of all countries’.79 Zhu and Wang argue that international governance of military AI is urgently needed and advocate for China to proactively contribute to the establishment of ethical norms, especially given the risks of misuse, strategic instability, and accountability gaps introduced by LAWS.80 Long and Xu further argue that a ‘Cold War logic’ informs the American perspective, and that being the first country to publish military AI guidelines responded to the U.S’. objective of maintaining hegemony over these processes, a point that is echoed by He et al. in their study of ethical thinking on the military applications of AI.81 The authors point to China’s shortcomings in not having formulated any such official document, which constrains the country’s ability to formulate norms globally. They thus recommend partnering with Russia and other countries to formulate shared military AI ethical norms in line with China’s and developing countries’ interests.82 Zhang and Du of the National University of Defense Technology further recommend that China should ‘exert its influence as a major country to participate in AIrelated negotiations under the UN framework’.83 The main challenges identified by Fu during Track-2 dialogues are AI-enabled weapons systems may cause excessive collateral damage and lead to escalating conflicts; biases present in certain technologies may provide decision makers with wrong recommendations; and the machine’s deficiencies in human cognitive capabilities, such as learning and common sense may increase the risk of battlefield conflicts or the escalation of international crises. China highlighted how ‘countries should assume legal responsibilities and be proactive in promoting international normbuilding on military actions involving AI’, as well as proactively establish ‘a threshold for human involvement . . . to make sure that the use of intelligent weapons does not cause superfluous injury’.84 China’s 2021 position paper on ‘Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence’ submitted to the UN CCW, acknowledges the ‘risks of military applications and even weaponization of AI’ and argues that ‘in terms of law and ethics, countries need to uphold the common values of humanity, put people’s well-being front and center, follow the principle of AI for good, and observe national or regional ethical norms in the development, deployment and use of relevant weapon systems’.85 In the previous position paper from 2018, unlike the U.S., Russia, Israel, France, the UK and others who explicitly rejected the ban on LAWS, China seemed supportive of the idea.86 However, China’s approach, which Kania argues is ‘characterized by a degree of strategic ambiguity and apparent preference for optionality’, is unlikely to stop China from developing such systems domestically.87 Supporting the ban rhetorically allows China to benefit from signalling diplomatic commitment to participating in international norm-building efforts.88 Crucially, however, the definition of LAWS adopted by China is extraordinarily narrow, making such a ban essentially inoperable; it would allow for a symbolic ban of systems with certain characteristics, whilst allowing for the development of weapons that, for instance, operate with a high degree of autonomy and limited human involvement but that are able to distinguish between legitimate and  llegitimate targets.89 As part of its efforts to shape international norms, in 2023 the U.S. Department of State published a declaration on military AI and autonomy, which neither China or Russia have signed.90 The case of Russia is, however, a useful example to contrast the role of the PRC in the global debates on military AI. The country seems unwilling to address the ethical issues brought about by AI and views international law as a ‘potential operational and strategic constraint’.91 Thus, while Russia appears to be regarding military AI overwhelmingly through the prism of military utility, China—as this article demonstrates—has showcased an interest in norms for regulating the use of military AI, although along normative lines that do not fully align with Western powers. This should be regarded as a cautiously positive signal in terms of China’s position, given that working for bilateral or multilateral agreements to regulate the use of AI on or off the battlefield remains crucial. While many countries seek to balance international cooperation with national security in the governance of military AI, China’s approach is distinctive in its strategic ambiguity. Unlike the U.S., which frames AI military ethics around preserving its global leadership and technological edge, or the EU, which adopts a human-centric and precautionary stance, China projects diplomatic support for international normbuilding—such as advocating a ban on LAWS—whilst ensuring the commitment is vague enough not to impinge on the pursuit of rapid AI militarization, through policies like military-civil fusion.92 This strategy of ambiguity allows China to position itself as a responsible stakeholder while retaining freedom to shape norms in ways that align with its geopolitical interests. The implications for global AI governance are significant: China’s involvement may lend legitimacy to multilateral efforts, but its narrow definitions and selective commitments could also undermine the development of robust, universally applicable norms.

Providing the first systematic mapping of Chinese debates on the ethics of military AI, this article finds that Chinese perspectives tend to coalesce around three recurring themes: the rejection of universal ethical norms; the insistence on Party-led human control; and the use of strategic ambiguity in balancing national security priorities with international norm-shaping efforts.

These themes frame how China internally debates the ethics of AI in warfare, while also revealing tensions that arise when engaging with global norm-making processes dominated by liberal democratic values

. Chinese writings—particularly those from military institutions—rarely frame debates in terms of Western ethical traditions such as human rights, proportionality, or just war theory. Instead, they tend to conceptualize ethics primarily as a governance and control challenge, focusing on accountability, restraint, and strategic stability. This does not imply outright opposition to principles like human rights or proportionality, but rather reflects a distinctive normative emphasis on sovereignty, Party leadership, and risk management.

Taken together, these three principles outline the dominant contours of China’s military AI ethics debates. Yet the ways in which they are interpreted and prioritized show some variation across different actor communities. While the three overarching principles identified in this article capture the dominant  contours of these debates, they should not be read as monolithic positions. Rather, they represent thematic nodes around which distinct actor groups have articulated partially overlapping yet at times divergent perspectives. Across these groups,
there is broad convergence on the need to uphold human control and responsibility in the use of military AI, even as tensions arise over the threshold and nature of that control

—military writings often promoting a ‘human-led, machine-assisted’ model that privileges operational flexibility, while academic voices advocate stricter ethical constraints and even bans on LAWS. Divergences also appear in the terminology used: political and military sources prefer the notion of ‘intelligentization’, whereas academic analyses more frequently employ the international framing of ‘autonomous weapons’, implying different ethical boundaries. Likewise, although all sides endorse notions of ‘harmony’ and pluralism, political discourse to a larger extent links ethics to Party leadership and national characteristics, while academics to a larger extent emphasizes international dialogue among diverse normative systems. On international governance, political and military texts align around cautious multilateralism and narrowly defined bans, in contrast with academic calls for proactive and transparent norm development. Finally, while all actors recognize the importance of accountability and risk mitigation, only academic and Track-2 sources discuss verification and testing mechanisms in concrete terms.

The resulting picture is one of structured convergence punctuated by selective tensions and latent contestation—a dynamic and evolving configuration of political, military, and academic debates that together delineate the emerging Chinese discourse on the ethics of military AI. By isolating the military dimension and examining overlapping yet distinct contributions from political, military, and academic actors, this article demonstrates that Chinese military AI ethics follows a trajectory that is related to, but not reducible to, China’s general AI ethics discourse. In doing so, it extends existing literature and advances theoretical understanding of how non-Western actors frame ethical debates in the military AI domain. It is important to stress that these perspectives do not represent a unified or monolithic ‘Chinese view’. As articulated above, political, military, and academic actors articulate similar concerns from distinct vantage points, and their discourses sometimes converge, overlap, or diverge. Likewise, ‘Western’ approaches to military AI ethics are themselves heterogeneous, ranging from human rights—oriented frameworks to operational doctrines of proportionality and just war.
